tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Recognize left-half-plane poles by using their negative real parts to identify decaying response modes that support BIBO stability in causal LTI systems.

image_slots.image_description: An $s$-plane with real/imaginary axes, labeled left and right half-planes, and one pole at $-2$, one pole at $2$, and one pole on the imaginary axis.

blocks.text: In the causal LTI setting from the prior lesson, pole placement is now the core signal for stability: the $s$-plane location of each pole drives time-domain behavior, and this step establishes that rule as a direct-instruction checkpoint.
Start with transfer-function poles. For $H(s)=\frac{N(s)}{D(s)}$, poles are the roots of $D(s)=0$. The left half-plane is defined by $\Re\{s\}<0$.
Use the base case $H(s)=\frac{1}{s+2}$ first: the denominator is zero at $s=-2$. Because $\Re\{-2\}=-2<0$, the associated mode is decaying. This is the canonical stable-decay anchor for this topic.

To connect pole location to mode shape, write a pole as $s=\sigma+j\omega$ so the time-domain factor is $e^{st}=e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}=e^{\sigma t}e^{j\omega t}$. The factor $e^{\sigma t}$ is the envelope, and strict negative $\sigma$ is what creates decay.

Boundary rule for this lesson: any pole with $\Re\{s\}\ge 0$ is outside the left-half-plane rule and breaks the causal-LTI BIBO-stability criterion used here. So the target action is explicit: all poles must satisfy $\Re\{s\}<0$.

The next sections reuse this same cue: identify poles from formulas, plot them on the $s$-plane, interpret the sign of each real part, then state the stability result from the same strict all-$\text{LHP}$ rule.

sections.section_title: Identifying Poles with Negative Real Parts

example_content.example_prompt: Classify the pole set $\{-1, -4, 2, -j3\}$ for the causal transfer function.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the rule that stability depends on the real part of each pole, so first convert every pole in the set to a $\sigma + j\omega$ form and keep the real part explicitly visible.
Apply the strict left-half-plane test from earlier: keep poles with $\Re\{s\}<0$. This gives $\{ -1, -4 \}$ as LHP poles and excludes $2$ and $0$.
Because the set contains the right-half-plane pole $2$, the strict all-$\Re\{s\}<0$ condition fails for this transfer function, so the result is not stable in this causal LTI-BIBO check.

sections.section_title: Locating Left-Half-Plane Poles on the s-Plane

image_slots.image_description: A pole-zero-like s-plane map with real axis Re(s) and imaginary axis Im(s). Include pole markers at $s=-2$, $s=-0$.5, $s=0$.2, and $s=-1+2j$, plus two zero markers at $s=\pm j2$, with clear coordinates and a clearly labeled imaginary-axis boundary.

example_content.example_prompt: Use the provided $s$-plane diagram to identify all left-half-plane poles and classify stability for the causal system.

explanation_blocks.text: The core cue is geometric: identify all pole locations on the given $s$-plane map and apply the same strict rule from earlier, $\Re\{s\}<0$, to each point.
Read the plotted poles: $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,0.2,\,-1+2j\}$, and ignore zero markers because this criterion depends on poles only.
Apply $\Re\{s\}<0$ to each pole. The poles in the LHP are $-2$, $-0.5$, and $-1+2j$; the pole at $0.2$ violates the strict inequality.
List of LHP poles: $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$. Because one pole is in the right half-plane, the all-poles rule fails, so this causal LTI example is classified as not BIBO stable.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Negative Real Parts as Decaying Modes

example_content.example_prompt: For poles $s=-2$ and $s=-1.5+2j$, write the associated mode terms in time-domain form and state whether each mode decays.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that each pole in Laplace form maps to a mode term $e^{st}$. For each pole, first write $s=\sigma+j\omega$ so the mode has the factored time-domain shape $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}=e^{\sigma t}e^{j\omega t}$, then test the sign of $\sigma$.
For $s=-2$, decomposition gives $\sigma=-2$, $\omega=0$, so the mode term is $e^{-2t}e^{j0t}=e^{-2t}$.

Both modes have strict negative real parts: $\sigma=-2<0$ and $\sigma=-1.5<0$, so both are decaying. The first decays faster because $|-2|>|-1.5|$, and $e^{-1.5t}e^{j2t}$ adds oscillation via frequency $\omega=2$ without changing decay.
The stability intuition is immediate: when all pole-derived modes have negative real parts, each response mode is bounded and decaying for causal LTI systems.

sections.section_title: Connecting All Left-Half-Plane Poles to BIBO Stability

example_content.example_prompt: Given $H(s)=\frac{10}{(s+1)(s+2)(s+4)}$, determine BIBO stability for a causal LTI system.

explanation_blocks.text: The target rule is the all-poles check: extract every pole from the denominator and test each one with $\Re\{s\}<0$. For $H(s)=\frac{10}{(s+1)(s+2)(s+4)}$, the poles come from $(s+1)(s+2)(s+4)=0$.
Now check each pole real part: $\Re(-1)=-1$, $\Re(-2)=-2$, and $\Re(-4)=-4$. Every pole is strictly negative.
Apply the strict all-pole rule from earlier: the system is BIBO stable only if every pole satisfies $\Re\{s\}<0$. Here all three satisfy it, so the transfer function is BIBO stable.
In one statement: all poles are in the left half-plane, so all modal terms are decaying for causal LTI and the whole transfer-function result is stable.

question_entry.lesson_core_move: Recognize left-half-plane poles by using their negative real parts to identify decaying response modes that support BIBO stability in causal LTI systems.

sections.section_title: Identifying Poles with Negative Real Parts

prompt_blocks.text: Given the pole set $\{-3, 0, 2, -0.5+j1\}$ for a causal LTI system, which classification is correct?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because three of the poles have negative real parts.
Not BIBO stable, because the pole at $0$ is on the boundary and the pole at $2$ is in the right half-plane.
BIBO stable, because the complex pole $-0.5+j1$ has a nonzero imaginary part.
Not BIBO stable, because stability depends on the imaginary part instead of the real part.
BIBO stable, because any negative pole is enough to make a causal LTI system stable.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Check the real parts pole by pole: $-3$, $0$, $2$, and $-0.5$. The strict BIBO test requires every pole to satisfy $\Re\{p\}<0$, and the poles at $0$ and $2$ fail that test.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the pole set $\{-4, -4, -0.5+j3, -0.5-j3\}$ for a causal LTI system, which classification is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Not BIBO stable, because the repeated pole at $-4$ counts twice.
BIBO stable, because every pole has negative real part.
Not BIBO stable, because complex poles are never allowed in the left half-plane.
Not BIBO stable, because the imaginary parts are nonzero.
BIBO stable, because repeated poles are stable even if one pole were on the boundary.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The repeated pole at $-4$ still satisfies the same sign test as a single pole, and the complex conjugate pair has real part $-0.5$. Since every pole has $\Re\{p\}<0$, the causal LTI system is BIBO stable.

sections.section_title: Locating Left-Half-Plane Poles on the s-Plane

image_slots.image_description: A pole-zero-style $s$-plane map with real axis labeled Re(s) and imaginary axis labeled Im(s). Show poles at $s=-2$, $s=-0.5$, $s=0.2$, and $s=-1+2j$, plus zero markers at $s=\pm j2$. Make the imaginary-axis boundary clear and the coordinates legible.

A pole-zero-style $s$-plane map with real axis labeled Re(s) and imaginary axis labeled Im(s). Show poles at $s=-2$, $s=-0.5$, $s=0$, and $s=-1+2j$, plus zero markers at $s=\pm j2$. Make the imaginary-axis boundary clear and the coordinates legible.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the pole map to identify the left-half-plane poles and choose the correct stability conclusion for the causal system.
Focus on poles only. The zeros on the imaginary axis are distractors here.

choice_blocks.text: LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,0.2,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is BIBO stable.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is not BIBO stable because of the pole at $0.2$.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is BIBO stable because the zeros lie on the imaginary axis.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,0.2,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is not BIBO stable because the pole at $-0.5$ is a zero.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is stable because any complex pole counts as left-half-plane.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the pole coordinates and apply the strict rule $\Re\{s\}<0$.
The left-half-plane poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$. The pole at $0.2$ has positive real part, so the all-poles test fails and the causal LTI system is not BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the pole map to identify the left-half-plane poles and choose the correct stability conclusion for the causal system.
Again, ignore the zeros and use only pole locations for the stability decision.

choice_blocks.text: LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j,\,0\}$, so the system is BIBO stable.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is BIBO stable because a pole at $0$ is still allowed.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,0\}$, so the system is not BIBO stable because the complex pole is ignored.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is not BIBO stable because the pole at $0$ lies on the imaginary axis and fails $\Re\{s\}<0$.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is not BIBO stable because zeros at $\pm j2$ are unstable.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the same strict left-half-plane rule to the plotted poles.
The left-half-plane poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$. The pole at $0$ sits on the imaginary axis, so it fails the strict inequality $\Re\{s\}<0$ and the causal LTI system is not BIBO stable.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Negative Real Parts as Decaying Modes

prompt_blocks.text: For poles $s=-1$ and $s=-2+3j$, which statement about the associated modes is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Both modes decay, and the $s=-2+3j$ mode decays faster because its real part is more negative.
The $s=-2+3j$ mode does not decay because the nonzero imaginary part makes it oscillatory.
The $s=-1$ mode decays faster because $|-1|<|-2|$.
The $s=-2+3j$ mode grows because the imaginary part is larger than the real part.
Both modes are non-decaying because every complex pole is unstable.

questions.correct_answer: Both modes decay, and the $s=-2+3j$ mode decays faster because its real part is more negative.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Write each pole as $s=\sigma+j\omega$ and look at the factor $e^{\sigma t}$. Here $\sigma=-1$ and $\sigma=-2$, so both modes decay. The more negative real part decays faster, and the imaginary part only adds oscillation.

prompt_blocks.text: For poles $s=-0.2+4j$ and $s=0.1$, which statement about the associated modes is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Both modes decay because one pole is complex and the other is real.
Only the $s=-0.2+4j$ mode decays; the $s=0.1$ mode grows because its real part is positive.
Both modes decay, and the $s=0.1$ mode decays faster because a smaller positive number is closer to zero.
The $s=-0.2+4j$ mode is non-decaying because the imaginary part is large.
The $s=0.1$ mode decays because real poles always decay if they are close to zero.

questions.correct_answer: Only the $s=-0.2+4j$ mode decays; the $s=0.1$ mode grows because its real part is positive.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A mode decays only when the real part $\sigma$ is negative. For $-0.2+4j$, $\sigma=-0.2$, so the mode decays with oscillation. For $0.1$, $\sigma=0.1>0$, so the mode grows and is not bounded.

sections.section_title: Connecting All Left-Half-Plane Poles to BIBO Stability

prompt_blocks.text: Determine BIBO stability of $H(s)=\frac{6}{(s+1)^2(s+0.2)(s+3)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable because every pole has negative real part, even though one pole is repeated.
Unstable because repeated poles are never stable.
Unstable because the pole at $-0.2$ is too close to the imaginary axis.
BIBO stable because the numerator is constant, so there are no zeros to worry about.
Unstable because the poles do not all have the same magnitude.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable because every pole has negative real part, even though one pole is repeated.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Factor the denominator to get poles at $s=-1$ (repeated), $s=-0.2$, and $s=-3$. Every pole has a negative real part, so the all-poles test says the causal LTI system is BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: Determine BIBO stability of $H(s)=\frac{4}{(s+2)(s-1)(s+5)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: Unstable because one pole is in the right half-plane.
BIBO stable because the two left-half-plane poles outweigh the one right-half-plane pole.
BIBO stable because the pole at $s=1$ is only one pole.
Unstable only if more than one pole is in the right half-plane.
BIBO stable because the numerator is constant, so the zeros do not matter.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable because one pole is in the right half-plane.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator gives poles at $s=-2$, $s=1$, and $s=-5$. The pole at $s=1$ has positive real part, so the all-poles test fails and the causal LTI system is not BIBO stable.
